crash.dup_check:
Checked /tmp/found_bugs.jsonl (3 entries: malformed-JSON-500 config dup, DATA_INTEGRITY_VIOLATION via like race at POST /api/recipes/:id/like, UNSAFE_CONTENT_TYPE via SVG upload at POST /api/recipes) and the "Already Filed" list (same malformed-JSON-500 entry, duplicated). None share this finding's primary class (CROSS_ACCOUNT_ACCESS) or route (DELETE /api/comments/:comment_id). Root cause here is specific to comment-deletion authorization (recipe-owner grant lets a session mutate/delete another user's comment row), unrelated to the like-race integrity bug, the SVG content-type bug, or the JSON body-parser 500. Not a duplicate.

Note on the finding itself: db.js's dbDeleteComment intentionally lets a recipe owner delete comments left by other users on their own recipe (comment at db.js:362: "a comment can be removed by whoever wrote it or by the owner of the recipe"). This PoC shows that this grant lets alice (owner of recipe 101, not the comment's author) issue a 2xx DELETE that removes bob's comment row with no relationship to bob's account other than "posted on alice's recipe" — the runner's ownership model (comment_id -> author only) treats this as one user mutating another user's row, and the route enforces no recipe-scoped consent from the comment author. Reproduced 3/3 with primary class CROSS_ACCOUNT_ACCESS.

verdict.evidence: PoC: alice logs in and DELETEs /api/comments/1. Comment 1 (seeded) belongs to bob but is attached to recipe 101, which alice owns. All 3 runs return status 200 and fire CROSS_ACCOUNT_ACCESS (actor=1, owner=2). However, /work/app/db.js's dbDeleteComment explicitly authorizes deletion by "row.user_id !== user_id && row.recipe_owner !== user_id" — i.e. the recipe owner is allowed to moderate/delete comments on their own recipe, a deliberate feature with its own audit-denial path for genuinely forbidden attempts. The oracle in run_poc.js checks only comment-author-vs-actor and ignores the recipe-owner exception the app itself implements, so it flags intended, authorized moderation as a cross-account violation. This is a false positive from the detector's model of ownership, not a real broken access control.
